newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Koreans disgruntled over president's speech - poll.
newsitem.headline: S.Koreans disgruntled over president's speech - poll.

text.p: Most South Koreans were disgruntled over President Kim Young-sam's apology for 1992 election spending abuses and said Kim should reveal details of his campaign financing, according to newspaper polls on Saturday.
President Kim apologised on a live television broadcast on Friday about deep-rooted corruption in Korean politics, but insisted he could not reveal details of his own campaign spending.

He also challenged opponents who accused him of over-spending in the 1992 presidential polls to clean up politics. and suggested they were just as guilty. His comments angered the opposition, which has vowed to fight Kim.
Surveys carried by most major dailies showed that the opposition's anger was shared by a majority of Koreans.

Joong-ang Ilbo, a major newspaper, said 80.6 percent of South Koreans were disgruntled about the president's speech. Another daily, the Hankook Ilbo, said 78.1 of Korean people thought the president's apology was insufficient.

Many South Koreans had expected a humble apology and some details of election funding abuses. But President Kim's attitude seemed calculated compared to his grave posture in February when he apologised for his son's behaviour and the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co under massive debts.

The steelmaker's failure revealed a web of corruption between Hanbo and top politicians that is now threatening Kim's presidency. The opposition alleges that Kim also partly bankrolled his campaign with 60 billion won ($67 million) from Hanbo.
The Joong-ang's survey showed that 82.6 percent of Koreans thought President Kim could reveal his election financing if he wanted to, an opinion that was echoed by the leading Chosun Ilbo's poll.

President Kim said spending abuses were a legacy of a corrupt past, adding: "You can very well imagine that nearly five years later it is impossible to account in detail for the total amount spent under such hectic circumstances".
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics immeditately blasted Kim as "pompous and confrontational", and vowed to wage war.
But National Congress leader Kim Dae-jung said his party had not decided whether to pressure the president to resign.

Chosun Ilbo's poll showed only 13.2 percent of Koreans wanted President Kim to step down before the end of his single-term in February next year, with 63.8 percent saying they would rather see Kim face legal action after his term.

According to prosecutor Kim Sung-ho, who put President Kim's immediate predecessors Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo behind bars for bribery and other crimes, Kim Young-sam could face legal action if any irregularities in spending were uncovered.
"But it will be difficult to send President Kim to jail for breaking the law on election campaign funding," Kim added.

Joong-ang Ilbo polls also showed South Koreans were pessimistic about political reforms, with 71.2 percent saying the campaign for December's presidential election in December would be no different from previous elections.
